A more literature-grounded reading of the September 22, 2021 FOMC statement is that the Fed is staying at the effective lower bound while relying on balance-sheet policies and forward guidance—tools widely endorsed in the post-crisis literature (Bernanke; Romer and Romer) and consistent with optimal, history-dependent policy in New Keynesian models (Svensson and Woodford, 2003; 2004). The explicit “makeup”/average-inflation-targeting framework announced at Jackson Hole 2020 (Powell) aims to anchor expectations at 2% by tolerating a period of inflation moderately above 2%, aligning with inflation-forecast targeting principles. The intent to begin tapering asset purchases “soon” reflects the literature’s guidance to recalibrate QE as “substantial further progress” is achieved while keeping rates low until maximum employment is in sight. That said, characterizing elevated inflation as “largely transitory” sits against a well-known credibility constraint: if inflation proves more persistent, the Taylor principle (Clarida) implies policy must ultimately respond forcefully to keep expectations anchored—echoing classic concerns about commitment and reputation (Sargent). Netting these factors, the tone is cautiously positive: improving activity and strong policy support, tempered by virus and inflation risks.
